conflict_topics: timing of cooking (weekday evenings vs after 7pm)
frequency of cooking (twice weekly vs once weekly)
impact on laundry and adjacent bedrooms
dialogue_quality_notes: Conversation is concise and pragmatic — participants give concrete reasons (work calls, laundry, cultural food).
Proposals evolved incrementally: timing → frequency → notification, showing iterative problem‑solving.
Minimal needless repetition; some positions were reiterated to clarify impact (B/C on laundry/room smell).
Cultural respect is present: Agent D framed the dish as family tradition, which redirected the discussion constructively.
evaluation.final_reason: Parties reached a concrete, mutual spoken agreement in Round 11: Agent D agreed to limit the dish to once on a weekend and to notify the flatmates in advance — “So I'll cook it once on a weekend, and I'll let you all know which day beforehand.” In return, Agent B agreed to close their door when told (“If you just tell me before you start, I can close my door.”) and Agent C agreed to avoid having laundry out on the notified day (“If you tell me which day ... I can just make sure I don't have laundry out then.”). Agent A had earlier accepted timing constraints (after 7 p.m.). All affected parties explicitly accepted these conditions in the transcript.
position_change_notes: Agent D shifted from routine twice‑weekly cooking to a concrete concession: cook once on a weekend and notify flatmates (Round 7 → Round 11).
Agent A moved from requesting a ban to accepting a timing/frequency compromise (initial ask → accepts after‑7pm and weekend plan).
Agent B initially supported a restriction but accepted a notification arrangement and closing their door when informed (Turn 21).
Agent C initially reported laundry being affected and ultimately accepted the arrangement to avoid hanging laundry on the notified weekend day (Turn 25 and Turn 29).

round_scores.evidence: Agent B: “I agree. My room's next to the kitchen and the smell gets into all my clothes.” Agent C: “Yeah, my laundry's out in the yard. It all smells of fish now.” (multiple housemates side with Agent A's complaint about Agent D's cooking)

Agent D challenges the implied restriction: “Other food makes smells also. Are we not going to cook curry? Or belacan?” Agent A responds by narrowing the complaint to long‑lasting smells and timing (work calls). This widens the scope of disagreement about what should be limited.
Agent B: “Yeah, that's it. The smell is still here from last night.” Agent C: “Exactly. I'm going to have to rewash everything.” (reinforcement of the core grievance; no settlement)

Agent D reframes the issue as timing: “Can we talk about when I cook it, instead of what I cook?” Agent A proposes a concrete time constraint: no strong smells on weekdays before 7 p.m. This reduces the scope of the conflict.
Agent D: “After 7 p.m. is okay. For the laundry, maybe I can just check with you before I cook?” Agent A: “Yeah, that sounds fair.” (partial agreement on timing and checking)

Agent B: “The time doesn't make a difference for me. The kitchen is right outside my door.” Agent C: “It's the same for me. I do my laundry in the evenings, so it's hanging out there after 7.” (timing solution is reported insufficient by two parties)
Agent D offers a frequency concession: “Okay. How about I only cook it once a week, on a weekend?” Agent A: “That works for me.” (frequency limitation reduces conflict for A but not yet for B/C)

Agent B: “But the smell will still fill up my room.” Agent C: “Yeah, same for my laundry. If it's out on the weekend, it'll still get the smell.” (the weekend proposal is still incompatible with B/C's needs)

Agent D asks how to proceed: “So what do you want me to do? Not cook it at all?” Agent B offers a concrete accommodation: “If you just tell me before you start, I can close my door.” (movement toward practical accommodations)

Agent D: “Okay, I can let you know.” Agent C: “If you tell me which day on the weekend you're going to cook, I can just make sure I don't have laundry out then.” (proposals for notification and behavior changes; most incompatibilities are being addressed but not all explicitly confirmed by everyone yet)

Agent D: “So I'll cook it once on a weekend, and I'll let you all know which day beforehand.” Agent C: “Okay, that works for me.” (clear, concrete mutual spoken agreement: D limits frequency to once on a weekend and will notify; others accept conditional accommodations)
No public speech or actions recorded; previous round contains an explicit, mutually accepted arrangement.

substantive_insights: Main tension was between cultural food practices and shared-space externalities (odor affecting bedrooms and laundry).
Timing constraints (no cooking during A's calls) helped some but did not solve others' problems (nearby rooms, evening laundry).
A durable solution combined limits on frequency + advance notification + behavioral accommodations (closing doors, avoiding laundry) rather than an outright ban.
Mutual concessions were required: the cook reduced frequency and agreed to coordination; others adjusted their habits on notified days.
